passage:
Ritu Api,
Confession time. Remember the eight thousand rupees the university refunded from my hostel deposit? Gone. In a week. A concert ticket, a smartwatch, dinner for five people.
The weird part is how careful I am with small things. I walk forty minutes to save a thirty-rupee auto. I skip the canteen tea because ten rupees adds up. I've been doing that all month and feeling very responsible.
Then tonight I added it up. All my walking and tea-skipping this month saved maybe six hundred rupees. The refund was eight thousand. It's like I have two wallets in my head: real money that I guard, and bonus money that doesn't count.
I'm not asking for money. I just needed to say it out loud. Next time something extra comes in, I'll ask Abbu to sit with me before I touch it.
Wasim

qa.a: The university refunded eight thousand rupees from the hostel deposit.

qa.q: Why did Wasim feel responsible while the refund vanished?
qa.a: Wasim felt proud and careful skipping tea and walking, while the refund felt like bonus money that didn't count, so the bigger loss went unnoticed.

qa.a: Asking Abbu to sit together before touching any extra money, so a trusted adult helps look at the whole picture.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel reading the confession?
qa.a: Ritu might feel amused and a little worried, and glad Wasim noticed the two wallets and is being honest.

grounding: Shows a student who spends a refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, as if the money sat in separate accounts.

Uday, you asked how I learned about money. I'm Raghav, and the lesson cost me a whole bonus.
During my internship, the company gave interns a surprise Diwali bonus of ten thousand rupees. I felt rich. That money wasn't real in my head. It was extra, like a gift. So I bought a leather jacket I wore twice, a gaming chair and a weekend in Goa.
Meanwhile I was obsessed with small costs. I argued with an autowala over ten rupees. I carried lunch from the hostel to avoid a sixty-rupee canteen thali.
In January my laptop died, and I needed twelve thousand. That's when I realised I'd never looked at all my money together. The bonus sat in one box in my head, the stipend in another, the canteen money in a third. If I'd seen it as one pile, I'd have kept the bonus for exactly this.
Now I write everything on one list, once a month. Boring. Works.

qa.q: How much was the surprise bonus?
qa.a: The bonus was ten thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Raghav spend the bonus so freely?
qa.a: Raghav felt rich and excited, treating the bonus as extra money like a gift, separate from the stipend.

qa.q: What does Raghav do now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Raghav writes all money on one list once a month, so the whole picture is visible before any spending.

qa.q: How might the autowala have seen the argument over ten rupees?
qa.a: The autowala probably found it petty and tiring, a fuss over ten rupees from someone who had just spent thousands.

grounding: Shows a student who spent a bonus carelessly while pinching on small costs, because separate mental accounts hid the whole picture.

April. Thomas got his first tax refund, six thousand rupees, from his part-time job. "Free money!" he told Raghav, and ordered new running shoes and a speaker the same night.
May. Thomas started counting every small thing. He refused Raghav's offer of a shared auto to save twenty rupees and walked home in the rain. He bought the cheapest biscuits. He felt very disciplined.
June. His college fee instalment was due, and he was short by four thousand. He stared at his banking app. "I've been so careful," he said.
Raghav scrolled through Thomas's spending with him. "Careful with twenty-rupee autos. Not with the six thousand."
Thomas sat back. He had never counted the refund as his money at all. That evening he wrote every rupee coming in and going out on one sheet, and took it to his father to talk it through.

qa.a: Thomas's tax refund was six thousand rupees.

qa.a: Thomas felt proud and careful counting small costs, while the refund had felt like free money that didn't count.

qa.a: Raghav sees that Thomas was careful with small autos but not with the big refund, and points it out plainly.

In the office pantry, Uday was complaining. "My bonus vanished again. And my salary account is always empty by the 25th. How are you never broke?"
Yogesh opened a spreadsheet on his phone. "One sheet. Everything I have and everything I owe, once a month. And every rupee coming in and going out, whatever it's called: salary, bonus, a gift from my aunt. To me, it's all one pool."
"But you have those labelled savings pots too. Trip, Laptop, Emergency."
"Those are just tools. They help me remember what the money is for. But when I decide anything, I look at the whole sheet first."
Uday frowned. "So the bonus doesn't feel like free money?"
"It feels nice. But it goes on the same sheet as the rent."
Uday took a photo of the column headings. "Can you show me this on Saturday?"

Dear Shalini,
Congratulations on your first salary! You asked how I manage mine, so here's what works for me. It isn't a rule for everyone, just what I've learned.
I used to keep money in boxes in my head. Salary money was serious. Diwali bonus was party money. Gifts from Nani were not really mine. I felt careful, but at the end of each year I had no idea where anything went.
Now, on the first of every month, I sit for half an hour and write one page: everything I have, everything I owe, what came in, what went out. Bonus, salary, gift, all on the same page. Only after that do I look at my little labelled pots, the trip fund and the laptop fund. They're useful, but they're not the whole picture.
Come over on your first Sunday and I'll show you my page. And if you want proper advice, the bank has a free adviser session. I went once and it helped.
Love,
Manjula Didi

Manoj, you asked what changed my relationship with money. I'm Devika, and it was one boring habit.
Once a month I make a single list. Not budgets in ten apps. One list: what I own, what I owe, what came in, what went out. My salary, my freelance payments, the money my grandmother slipped me at the wedding, all of it goes on the same list. I used to treat gift money like it wasn't real, and freelance money like a treat. That's how I ended up with a card bill I couldn't explain.
I still have labelled accounts: one for rent, one for my sister's college gift, one for travel. They're like drawers. Handy. But I don't let the drawers fool me into thinking I'm richer or poorer than I am. I look at the whole cupboard first.
If a listener wants to start, take one evening, one page, and if the numbers scare you, sit with someone you trust or a proper adviser.

Last winter, before our school's Christmas play, I learned something about my brain. I'm Sharmila, and I was in charge of the props.
Vidya Ma'am told me all the prop jobs in one go: the star goes on stage in scene one, the lamb comes out in scene two, the gifts go under the tree after the song, the lantern is lit before the last scene, and the chair gets moved back. I nodded as if I understood everything.
In scene one I got the star right. After that, my head was empty. The lamb came out late. The lantern never got lit.
After the play, Ma'am didn't scold. She said, "That was too much at once for anyone." The next year she wrote each job on a card, in order, and stuck them on the backstage wall. I didn't miss a single one.

qa.a: Sharmila got the star right in scene one.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel after scene one?
qa.a: Sharmila felt blank and flustered, as the long list of jobs had slipped out of memory.

qa.q: What did Vidya Ma'am do the next year, and why did it work?
qa.a: She wrote each job on a card in order on the backstage wall, so Sharmila didn't have to hold them all in memory.

qa.q: How did Vidya Ma'am see the mistakes?
qa.a: Ma'am saw them as too much for anyone at once, not as carelessness, and didn't scold.

Swimming camp note, May. Written by Deepak, coach.
Today I gave the beginners six things to remember at once: kick from the hips, keep your face in the water, breathe to the side, reach long, pull under your body, and don't stop at the wall. Binita nodded and jumped in.
She kicked beautifully for five metres, then lifted her head, forgot to breathe to the side, and stood up coughing. "I forgot the rest," she said, embarrassed.
She hadn't forgotten because she wasn't listening. Six instructions is too many for anyone learning something new.
What I did next: I gave her one thing only. "Just kick, face in, for one length." She did it perfectly. Tomorrow we'll add breathing. One new thing a day.

qa.q: How many things did Deepak give the beginners to remember?
qa.a: Deepak gave the beginners six things to remember at once.

qa.q: How did Binita feel when she stood up coughing?
qa.a: Binita felt embarrassed and flustered, having forgotten the rest of the six instructions.

qa.q: What did Deepak change, and why does it help?
qa.a: One instruction at a time, just kick with face in for one length, adding one new thing a day, which fits what a learner can hold.

qa.q: How does Deepak understand Binita's forgetting?
qa.a: Deepak sees it as normal overload from too many instructions, not a lack of listening.

grounding: Shows, in a coach's note, a child who forgets most of a long list of instructions and succeeds with one short step.

In the school library's study hour, Nitin sat with his chemistry book, earphones in, a Punjabi playlist on and his phone face-up on the table. It buzzed every two minutes: the class group, a cousin, a game notification.
He read the paragraph on isomers four times. Each time, a line of a song or a buzz cut in, and the words slid off.

Nitin couldn't answer a single question on isomers. "I read it four times!"
"You read it with a concert and a phone party going on," Ira said. "Tomorrow, try with the phone in your bag and no songs with words. Instrumental, if you need something."
The next day Nitin tried. In forty minutes he got through the whole topic, and when Ira quizzed him, he got seven out of ten.

Sahil,
You asked why my marks jumped this term. Honestly, it's embarrassing how simple it was.
Last term I studied on my bed with the TV on in the next room, my phone beside me and music with lyrics in my ears. I thought I was studying for three hours every night. But in tests, whole chapters were blank. I felt stupid.
Then our physics teacher said something in class: your brain can hold only a few things at once, and every buzz and every lyric takes a slot. So I tried an experiment. One evening: phone in Mummy's room, no music, desk instead of bed, fifty minutes.
I learned more in those fifty minutes than in three noisy hours. It was almost annoying.
Try it before your exams. Put your phone somewhere it can't see you.
Ritu

Parveen, you wanted a study story for the podcast? I'm Ujjwal, Class 12, and I ran an experiment on myself.
I always studied with rap on and my phone next to the book. I told everyone I could focus fine. Then I'd open the history chapter the next morning and it was as if I'd never seen it.
So I tried two evenings. Evening one: normal. Music with lyrics, phone buzzing, replying as I went. Evening two: phone in the kitchen, no music, just the book and a notebook.
The next morning my sister quizzed me on both chapters. Evening one: three out of ten. Evening two: eight out of ten.
Same brain, same time, same chair. The only difference was how many things were fighting for space in my head. Every buzz, every rap line, was taking a seat the history needed.
I still listen to rap. Just not while I study.

As the new block development officer for eleven villages near Barabanki, Noor had a hundred things coming at her every day: water-tanker complaints, school repairs, pension forms, visits from the district office.
In her first month she tried to hold it all in her head and forgot a pension camp. An old woman waited in the sun for three hours. Noor never forgot her face.
So she changed how she worked. Every morning she wrote the day on a single sheet: three big jobs, broken into small steps. "Fix school roof" became "call the contractor", "check the budget", "visit Thursday". She switched off group notifications from ten to one, and told Zeenat, her assistant, to interrupt only for emergencies. At two she drank tea under the neem tree for ten minutes, no phone.
By the third month the district office noticed fewer complaints. Zeenat noticed that Noor laughed more.

qa.q: How many villages did Noor handle?
qa.a: Noor handled eleven villages near Barabanki.

qa.q: Why did Noor never forget the old woman's face?
qa.a: Noor felt ashamed and sorry that forgetting the pension camp left the woman waiting three hours in the sun.

qa.q: How did Noor lighten the load on her mind?
qa.a: A single morning sheet with three big jobs broken into steps, notifications off from ten to one, interruptions only for emergencies, and a ten-minute break at two.

qa.q: What did Zeenat notice by the third month?
qa.a: Zeenat noticed that Noor laughed more, which suggests the new way of working made her calmer.

Rosa's first big project at the architecture studio in Mexico City had forty drawings due in three weeks, and by the fourth day she was answering emails at midnight and waking at four with lists spinning in her head.
Dalia, the senior architect at the next desk, watched for a week, then brought her a coffee. "Want to see what I do?"
Dalia's method was almost boring. A paper notebook for every task the moment it appeared. Each drawing broken into four steps on a sticky note. Email checked at eleven and at four, not in between. A walk round the block after lunch.
Rosa tried it. The first two days felt slow. Then she noticed she wasn't waking at four any more, and on Friday she caught a mistake in a stair drawing she'd have missed the week before.
She finished the forty drawings a day early, and stuck her own four-step sticky notes on Dalia's screen as a thank-you.

qa.a: Rosa felt overwhelmed and restless, answering emails at midnight and waking at four with lists spinning.

It was the last week of the quarter at the insurance office, and Jyoti had exactly one hour to train Sangeeta, the new claims assistant, before the rush.
She started the way she'd been trained herself: the whole system in one go. Codes, forms, deadlines, exceptions, three software screens. Twenty minutes in, she noticed Sangeeta's pen had stopped moving. Her eyes had the glassy look of someone who has stopped taking anything in.
Jyoti stopped. She remembered that look on her own face, two years ago.
"Okay. Forget everything I just said," she said. "Today you'll do one kind of claim only: travel claims. Here's one I did yesterday as an example. Here's a five-step checklist. Try three, and I'll check them with you at twelve."
Sangeeta's shoulders came down. By twelve she had done four, one with a small mistake they fixed together. On Friday, Jyoti added the second kind of claim.

qa.q: How many travel claims had Sangeeta done by twelve?
qa.a: Sangeeta had done four travel claims by twelve.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel when she noticed Sangeeta's glassy look?
qa.a: Jyoti felt a jolt of recognition and concern, remembering the same overwhelmed look on her own face two years earlier.

qa.q: How did Jyoti change the training, and why did it work?
qa.a: Jyoti cut it to one kind of claim, gave an example and a five-step checklist, and time to practise, so Sangeeta wasn't overloaded.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel once the training changed?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt relieved, her shoulders coming down, and managed four claims with growing confidence.

On Mahima's first day at the Pune software firm, her team lead, Vikas, noticed something at lunch. She had a notebook with eleven pages of scribbles, a laptop with twenty tabs open, and she hadn't touched her food.
"Everyone's been sending you links, haven't they?" he asked.
She nodded, a little desperately. "The code rules, the testing rules, the release calendar, the old project, the new project... I don't know what matters."

"Okay, Joseph, today you'll learn the whole breakfast station," said the head cook, reeling it off. "Eggs four ways, dosa batter ratio, idli steamer timing, buffet refills, allergy labels, the—"
Jagdish, the senior cook, touched her arm. "Chef, can I take him?"
She shrugged and moved on.
Jagdish turned to Joseph, who was holding a ladle as if it might bite. "How much of that did you catch?"
"Eggs. Something about batter."
"Honest. Good. Today, only eggs. Watch me do four plates. Then you do four. Here's a card with the four kinds. Tomorrow, dosa."
"Only eggs?"
"Only eggs. When eggs are easy, your head has room for the next thing."
By the end of the morning Joseph had made thirty perfect omelettes and was grinning. "Tomorrow, dosa?"
"Tomorrow, dosa," Jagdish said.

qa.a: Only eggs today: watch four plates, try four, use a card of the four kinds, and dosa tomorrow, so each skill has room to settle.

During the wheat harvest, the courtyard was full of noise: the thresher, the chickens, the neighbours shouting. Sahil, two, sat in the dust pushing his little red tractor. "Brrrm."
"Sahil! Sahil, come, milk!" called his mother, Zeenat.

In the flat in Barcelona, Noa, two, was stacking blocks, her tongue poking out.
"Noa! Noa! Look at my drawing!" shouted her big brother Alejandro, waving the paper right beside her.
Noa put another block on top. She didn't turn.
"She's ignoring me!" Alejandro cried.
Their mother knelt down. "She's not ignoring you. Her whole head is in the tower right now. Watch." She waited until the tower fell, then said softly, "Noa, look."
Noa turned, saw the drawing and clapped. Alejandro grinned.

qa.a: Alejandro felt hurt and frustrated, thinking Noa was ignoring him, until she clapped.

At Thursday's clown show, Darshan sat at the front, eyes fixed on the clown's red nose. Halfway through, a dog wandered across the stage. Every other child pointed.

In science week last winter, our teacher showed us a video of children passing a basketball. "Count the passes by the team in white," she said. I'm Avni, and I love counting, so I stared hard.
Fifteen passes. I was so proud.
Then Ma'am asked, "Who saw the bear?"
Half the class put up their hands, laughing. My friend Mahima said a person in a bear suit walked right through the middle and waved!
I didn't believe her. We watched it again. There it was: a big brown bear, waving at the camera for ages.
I felt so silly. But Ma'am said it wasn't about being silly. When your attention is busy counting, your eyes can look right at something and not see it.

qa.q: How many passes did Avni count?
qa.a: Avni counted fifteen passes.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when the bear appeared on the second watch?
qa.a: Avni felt silly and amazed, having looked right at the screen and still missed the bear.

qa.q: What did Ma'am explain, and how could Avni use it?
qa.a: That busy attention can miss something the eyes are looking at, so Avni can remember that focusing on one task can hide others.

qa.q: How did Mahima experience the video?
qa.a: Mahima noticed the bear and laughed, and had to convince Avni it was there.

grounding: Shows a child counting passes in a video who misses a bear crossing the screen, because attention decides what is seen.

passage:
Class 4 note, the week before Holi. Written by Bhavna, sports teacher.
At practice I asked the children to count how many times their partner bounced the ball. Parveen counted with total focus, lips moving.
Meanwhile the principal walked across the field carrying a huge tray of gujiyas for the Holi celebration and stood beside me for a whole minute. The children shrieked. Parveen didn't look up once. "Forty-two bounces!" she announced.
When I told her about the gujiyas, she stared at me. "The principal was here? Where?"
Her eyes were open. She just wasn't looking with her attention.
What I did next: I told the class that attention is like a torch; where you point it, you see. Then we all ate gujiyas, and Parveen got two.

qa.q: How many bounces did Parveen count?
qa.a: Parveen counted forty-two bounces.

qa.q: Why didn't Parveen notice the principal?
qa.a: Parveen felt determined and absorbed in counting, so her attention didn't take in the principal, even with her eyes open.

qa.q: What did Bhavna teach the class, and how could it help?
qa.a: That attention is like a torch, you see where you point it, which helps children understand why they miss obvious things.

qa.q: How did the other children react to the principal?
qa.a: The other children shrieked with excitement at the tray of gujiyas.

grounding: Shows, in a teacher's note, a child so busy counting bounces that she misses the principal carrying gujiyas across the field.

25 December, night.
Dear diary, today Jahnavi Didi came home from hostel with her hair cut really short. She sat next to me for an hour while I played my racing game, and I didn't notice. Not even when she said, "Notice anything?"
I said, "No, why?" without looking.
At dinner Mummy said, "Doesn't Didi look nice?" I looked up and nearly dropped my spoon. Her hair was gone!
Didi laughed so much. She said I had looked right at her three times.
I think my eyes saw her but my brain was in the race. Scary. What if I miss something important like that?
Tomorrow I'm going to play only after lunch, and look at people when they talk.
Saurabh
